questions.prompt: Put these stages of the expense lifecycle, per Lesson 1, in the correct order.
items: Incur — an employee spends money on a business cost
Capture — the expense is recorded manually, from a card feed, or via receipt imaging
Submit — the employee assembles items into an expense report and submits it
Audit and approve — audit rules run automatically and a human approver reviews the report
Account — Expenses creates the accounting distributions for the General Ledger
Reimburse — Expenses hands off to Payables, which pays the employee or the card issuer
questions.explain: Every expense report moves through the same six stages in this order: incur, capture, submit, audit and approve, account, reimburse. Expenses never pays anyone directly — accounting happens before reimbursement, and reimbursement itself is handed off to Payables.

questions.prompt: A new consultant wants to configure audit rules first for a new business unit, since audit rules feel like the most important part of the setup. Per Lesson 2's setup sequence, what actually happens if audit rules are built before expense report templates and expense types exist?
options: There is nothing yet for an audit rule to evaluate, since audit criteria reference expense types and report data that don't exist until templates and types are set up first
Audit rules are designed to be configured first, before templates, since they define company-wide risk policy that templates must then conform to
Audit rules can be built in any order relative to templates, since both are scoped only to the business unit and have no other dependency
The system automatically creates placeholder expense types the moment an audit rule references one that doesn't exist yet
questions.explain: Lesson 2 is explicit that later setup steps depend on earlier ones: you cannot define an audit rule against expense types and reports that don't exist yet. Experienced consultants build the sequence top-down — system options, templates and types, conversion rates, policies, audit rules, approval rules, card programs — rather than jumping ahead to the parts that feel more interesting.

questions.prompt: Match each Chapter 1 setup term to what it actually is.
right: A seeded, system-defined grouping like Hotel, Airfare, or Meals that drives behaviors such as itemization eligibility
The specific claimable item nested inside a category, such as Hotel or Motel, each carrying its own policy limit
The scope at which nearly every Expenses setup object, including templates, policies, and audit rules, is independently defined
The business-unit-scoped set of expense types an employee can pick from, which also carries default accounting information
questions.explain: A template is the business-unit-scoped container of expense types that also carries default accounting information. A category is a seeded grouping (Hotel, Airfare, Meals) that drives system behavior. A type is the specific thing an employee picks inside a category, each with its own limit. A business unit is the scope almost every one of these setup objects is defined under, since different parts of a company legitimately need different rules.

questions.prompt: Marcus Webb submits a $410 client dinner against a $300 policy limit for Business Meal — Client Present. Per Lesson 4, which outcome correctly describes what happens to his expense report?
options: The item is blocked from submission entirely until Marcus removes it or lowers the amount to $300 or less
The system flags the item as over policy, requires Marcus to enter a justification, and still allows the report to submit, routing it for mandatory audit review
The report submits normally with no flag at all, since Castellan's policy limits only apply to Hotel and Mileage expense types
The $410 amount is automatically reduced to $300 on submission, with the remaining $110 silently dropped from the claim
questions.explain: Most Castellan policy limits are soft limits, not hard stops. An over-policy item like Marcus's dinner gets flagged, requires a typed justification, and still submits — but it's routed for mandatory audit review rather than passing through invisibly. A true hard limit that blocks submission entirely is reserved for a small number of company-wide prohibitions.

questions.prompt: Castellan Supply Co. issues both individual-liability and company-liability corporate cards. For a company-liability card charge on an approved expense report, who does Payables actually pay?
options: The employee, because an individual-liability card makes the employee personally responsible to the card issuer
Neither; the amount is held as a non-reimbursable tracking entry until the card issuer's statement closes
The card issuer, because Castellan itself is responsible for the balance on a company-liability card
The employee, because Castellan itself is responsible for the balance on a company-liability card
The card issuer, because every corporate card charge is paid to the issuer regardless of liability type
The employee's manager's cost center, which reimburses the card issuer on the employee's behalf
questions.explain: On a company-liability card, Castellan itself owes the balance to the card issuer, so Payables pays the card issuer directly and the employee is never reimbursed for that line, since they never personally paid for it. On an individual-liability card, the reasoning flips: the employee owes the issuer, so Payables reimburses the employee instead.
questions.distractorExplain: Option 4 is the exact mirror image of the correct answer: it keeps the right justification sentence — 'Castellan itself is responsible for the balance' — but swaps who actually gets paid. Lesson 9 draws this distinction specifically so a consultant doesn't get it backwards: company-liability means the issuer gets paid, not the employee. Option 5 makes the opposite mistake in the other direction, erasing the liability distinction entirely by claiming the issuer is always paid regardless of card type — which ignores that individual-liability and cash expenses do reimburse the employee.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about receipts and itemization, per Lesson 6.
options: An employee without a receipt is automatically blocked from submitting the expense item entirely
A missing receipt declaration is a formal electronic statement affirming the expense occurred and the amount is accurate
Itemization splits a single bundled receipt, like a hotel folio, into multiple expense items each coded to its own expense type
An attachment and a required receipt are the same requirement — the two terms are interchangeable in Expenses
A payment hold rule can place current or future expense reports on hold company-wide for an employee with too many missing-receipt declarations
questions.explain: A missing receipt declaration lets an employee submit without the physical receipt by affirming the expense occurred, rather than being blocked outright. Itemization splits a bundled receipt like a hotel folio into correctly coded pieces. Castellan's payment hold rule does place reports on hold company-wide once missing-receipt declarations pile up past a threshold. A receipt and an attachment are explicitly different things: a receipt is required proof backing a dollar amount, while an attachment is optional supporting documentation.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: Jordan Reyes receives a $600 cash advance but only incurs $410 of qualifying business expense. After the advance is applied against the expense report, Jordan owes the company $________.
questions.explain: The expense report applies the full $600 advance against the $410 total, producing a negative net amount: $600 - $410 = $190 that Jordan owes back, collected through a future deduction, a payroll deduction, or a manual repayment depending on how the business unit is configured.

questions.prompt: Castellan uses per diem for most domestic travel and itemized meal receipts for international trips. Per Lesson 7, why does the course say this split makes sense, rather than picking one method for every trip?
options: Per diem is simpler to audit domestically since there are no receipts to check, while actual meal costs on international trips vary too widely for a single rate schedule to be fair
Per diem is legally required for any trip inside the company's home country, while itemized receipts are legally required for international trips
Oracle Fusion Expenses has not yet published per diem rate schedules for any country outside the United States
Mixing both methods for the same trip is the recommended approach, so combining per diem domestically with itemized receipts internationally maximizes what an employee can claim
questions.explain: The course gives two concrete reasons for the split: per diem is simpler to audit domestically because there's nothing to check beyond dates and destination, and itemized receipts are used internationally because actual costs vary too widely for one schedule to be fair. The warning about 'mixing both' in Lesson 7 refers to using both methods on the very same trip, which creates duplicate claims — it is not an endorsement of combining them across different trip types.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of the cash advance process, per Lesson 8, in the correct order.
items: The employee submits a cash advance request specifying an amount and business purpose tied to an upcoming trip
The request routes for approval, generally to the same manager who approves the employee's expense reports
Castellan pays the approved advance through Payables as a standalone payment to the employee
The employee later submits an expense report, and Expenses displays an Apply Cash Advances prompt
The employee applies the outstanding advance against the report, or justifies not applying it, producing the net reimbursement or amount owed
questions.explain: A cash advance is requested and approved before any spending happens, paid through the same Payables infrastructure used for reimbursements, and only later applied against an actual expense report at the header level — which is also the point where a shortfall (owing money back) or a normal net reimbursement gets calculated.

questions.prompt: An approver rejects one expense report, and on a different report, an approver instead chooses 'request more information.' Per Lesson 13, which statement correctly distinguishes what happens next in each case?
options: Both actions return the report to the employee in a fully editable state, and both restart audit and approval from the beginning once resubmitted
Request more information is only available for reports that have already been accounted, never before accounting has happened

Rejection returns the report to the employee in a fully editable state and restarts audit and approval from the beginning on resubmission; request more information pauses the report at its current point and resumes from there once the employee responds, without restarting the full sequence
Rejection can only be performed by an audit rule configured to reject automatically — a human approver is never allowed to reject a report directly
Rejection permanently closes the report with no possibility of resubmission, while request more information allows unlimited resubmission attempts

Rejection pauses the report at its current point and resumes from there once the employee responds; request more information returns the report to the employee in a fully editable state and restarts audit and approval from the beginning
questions.explain: Rejection sends a report all the way back: the employee gets full editing rights, and resubmission restarts audit and approval from scratch, since a rejected-then-resubmitted report isn't assumed fine just because it was reviewed once. Request more information is deliberately lighter — it pauses the report at its current point to ask a specific question and resumes from there once answered, without restarting the whole sequence. Castellan's approvers reserve full rejection for when something is actually wrong, and use the lighter option for small clarifications.
questions.distractorExplain: Option 6 keeps the right overall shape — one action does a full restart, the other does a lighter pause-and-resume — but swaps which action does which. It's rejection that hands the report back fully editable and restarts the whole cycle; request more information is the pause-and-resume that never restarts anything. Getting these two backwards is exactly the mistake this lesson's distinction is meant to prevent.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about expense audit rules, per Lesson 10.
options: An audit list rule triggers automatically based on configured criteria, without requiring a human to decide whether to flag a report in the first place
Every audit rule evaluates only a single report in isolation; none of them can look at an employee's pattern across multiple past reports
'Reject expense report' sends a report straight back to the employee without first routing it to an auditor
Audit rules and manager approval are the same workflow step, just described with two different names
'Waive receipts' and 'waive receipts and complete audit' both exist as configurable actions and can be used selectively, for example for a trusted long-tenured employee
questions.explain: Audit list rules fire automatically on their configured criteria, with no human deciding whether to flag a given report. 'Reject expense report' is specifically used for clear-cut violations and skips the auditor's worklist entirely. Waive-receipts actions exist and are used selectively. Castellan actually uses both report-level rules (evaluating one report alone) and employee-level rules (evaluating a pattern across history), so rules are not limited to single-report evaluation. Audit rules and manager approval are also explicitly distinct, sequential steps, not the same thing with two names.

questions.prompt: A Castellan expense report includes items charged to 'Project Falcon.' Per Lesson 11, which predefined approval rule set is specifically responsible for routing that portion of the approval to the project's manager, running in parallel with the employee's supervisor approval?
options: ExpenseReportRuleSet
CostCenterRuleSet
ProjectManagerRuleSet
ExpenseRuleSet
questions.explain: ProjectManagerRuleSet routes to the relevant project manager(s) when expense items are charged to a project, running in parallel with other applicable rule sets. ExpenseReportRuleSet routes to the supervisor, CostCenterRuleSet routes to cost center owners, and ExpenseRuleSet routes to a type-based specialist — none of which is specifically project-based.

questions.prompt: Match each predefined approval rule set, per Lesson 11, to what it actually routes an approval to.
right: A specialist approver based on expense type, such as a Travel Manager approving air travel booked outside the preferred agency
The employee's supervisor, via the HR supervisor hierarchy
The project manager(s), when expense items are charged to a project
The owner(s) of the cost center the report will post to, running in parallel across multiple cost centers if needed
questions.explain: ExpenseReportRuleSet routes to the supervisor hierarchy — the default most companies start from. CostCenterRuleSet routes to cost center owners, in parallel if a report spans several. ProjectManagerRuleSet routes to project managers for project-charged items. ExpenseRuleSet routes to a specialist approver based on expense type. Castellan combines the first two, running supervisor and cost-center-owner approval together whenever a report crosses cost centers.

questions.prompt: Priya's $275 Hotel item was captured from a company-liability corporate card transaction. Per Lessons 9 and 14, which journal entry correctly reflects how Expenses accounts for it through Subledger Accounting?
options: Debit Travel & Lodging Expense $275; Credit Corporate Card Payable $275
Debit Travel & Lodging Expense $275; Credit Employee Expense Payable $275
Debit Corporate Card Payable $275; Credit Travel & Lodging Expense $275
Debit Cash $275; Credit Travel & Lodging Expense $275
questions.explain: The expense account debited is the same regardless of payment method, but a company-liability card charge credits Corporate Card Payable rather than Employee Expense Payable, since Castellan itself — not the employee — owes the card issuer. Employee Expense Payable is the credit used for cash expenses and individual-liability card charges instead.

questions.prompt: Put these stages of Marcus Webb's $410 client dinner, per Lesson 15's full trail, in the correct order.
items: Marcus enters the Business Meal — Client Present expense item with a justification for the over-policy amount
The item is audited and approved through BPM
Subledger Accounting creates the accounting event: debit Client Entertainment Expense, credit Employee Expense Payable
Process Expense Reimbursement creates a Payables invoice for $410.00, payee Marcus Webb
A Payment Process Request pays the invoice, generating a payment entry that clears the liability
Both the accounting event and the payment entry post as journal entries to the General Ledger
questions.explain: The trail runs through three systems in a fixed order: Expenses (the item itself, then audit and approval), Subledger Accounting and Payables (the accounting event, then the invoice, then the payment), and finally the General Ledger, where both the accounting event and the payment entry land as journal entries. A consultant tracing a GL discrepancy has to know which stage produced which record.

questions.prompt: Jordan Reyes's 40-mile round-trip mileage claim reimburses less than expected. Per Lesson 17's Ticket 1, what was actually wrong, and does fixing it also correct Jordan's already-processed claim?
options: The mileage rate schedule's effective date was entered a week too late, so the new $0.67 rate wasn't active yet; fixing the schedule's effective date corrects all future claims, but Jordan's already-processed claim still needs a separate manual correction
The mileage rate schedule's effective date was entered a week too late; fixing the schedule's effective date automatically reprocesses and corrects Jordan's already-submitted claim at the same time
Jordan entered the wrong number of miles on the claim, which is a data-entry error unrelated to the rate schedule
The claim is correct as paid; Castellan's mileage policy intentionally withholds a portion of the standard rate
questions.explain: The root cause was the rate schedule's effective date being entered a week too late, so Jordan's claim processed under the old $0.65 rate instead of the new $0.67 rate. Fixing the schedule's effective date prevents the problem going forward, but per Lesson 13's correction rules, it does not retroactively fix Jordan's specific already-processed claim — that needs its own manual correction.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank with the acronym: ________ lets a power user or consultant build ad hoc analysis on top of live Expenses data, dragging in exactly the dimensions a question needs, instead of being limited to Oracle's seeded reports.
questions.explain: OTBI (Oracle Transactional Business Intelligence) lets someone cross dimensions like expense type, employee, cost center, date range, and policy violation flag however a specific question demands, built on the same underlying data Expenses and Subledger Accounting already captured — something no fixed seeded report can anticipate.

questions.prompt: Designing policy for Harrowgate Freight Logistics, the consultant concentrates audit intensity on fuel card misuse and unsubstantiated client meals rather than spreading scrutiny evenly across every expense type. Per Lesson 18, why?
options: Because those are the two risk areas discovery actually surfaced as historical pain points, and auditing everything equally would waste reviewer time on low-risk spend while the named risk areas get no extra scrutiny
Because Oracle Fusion Expenses technically limits any business unit to configuring at most two high-risk audit rules
Because client meals and fuel card charges are always the highest-dollar items on any expense report, regardless of what discovery reveals
Because Harrowgate's CFO requires 100% audit coverage on every expense type, and two is the maximum rate Oracle allows a rule to reach
questions.explain: Discovery surfaced fuel card misuse and unsubstantiated client meals as Harrowgate's actual historical complaints, so policy design concentrates audit effort there rather than spreading it evenly. Routine ground transportation and standard in-policy hotel stays are deliberately left with lighter scrutiny, since nothing in discovery suggested those were a problem — audit intensity follows actual risk, not a uniform default.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about corporate card reconciliation, per Lesson 19.
options: The three-way match compares what the card issuer billed, what arrived in Expenses as transactions, and what has been attached to approved expense reports
A persistent, growing gap between these three numbers signals a problem with the program's operational health, not necessarily any single bad transaction
A disputed charge is resolved inside Expenses directly, using the same audit list rule that handles policy violations
For a terminated employee with an unassigned balance, the standard resolution is payroll offset or direct collection, following the company's offboarding policy
A duplicate feed transaction is always the employee's fault, and is resolved by rejecting their next expense report
questions.explain: The three-way match and the 'a growing gap signals an operational problem' framing are both exactly how Lesson 19 describes reconciliation, and offboarding offset/collection is the stated resolution for a departed employee's unassigned balance. A disputed charge actually routes to the card issuer's own dispute process, outside Expenses entirely — not an audit list rule. A duplicate feed transaction is described as a feed configuration problem the consultant works with the issuer's technical contact to fix, not an employee error to penalize.

questions.prompt: Castellan US Operations' monthly reconciliation shows: issuer statement total $184,620.00; transactions received in the feed $184,620.00; amount attached to approved expense reports $179,310.00. Per Lesson 19, what does this specific pattern indicate?
options: The issuer and the feed agree, so the $5,310 gap is downstream of the feed — in employees not yet attaching and completing the lifecycle for those transactions, not a feed or issuer discrepancy
The card issuer's statement itself must be wrong, since it should match the attached-to-approved-reports total exactly every single month
The transaction feed failed to deliver $5,310 worth of charges that the issuer billed, which is a feed configuration problem Castellan must escalate immediately
This pattern is impossible — Oracle Fusion Expenses does not allow these three numbers to differ under any circumstances
questions.explain: Because the issuer total and the feed total match exactly, the feed and the issuer agree — the gap sits only between the feed and what's actually been attached to approved reports. That points to the normal lag of employees not yet finishing the lifecycle on those transactions, not a feed or issuer problem. A short lag is expected in a healthy program; a persistent, growing version of this same gap is what would actually warrant concern.
